By the end of this lesson I will be able to

  • Describe what a mixture is.
  • Explain the difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures.
  • Give examples of each type of mixture.
  • Carry out the elephant toothpaste experiment safely and explain the foam.
The big ideaA mixture is two or more substances mixed but NOT chemically joined. Homo means SAME: you cannot see the parts. Hetero means DIFFERENT: you can.
SafetyGoggles and gloves: hydrogen peroxide can irritate eyes and skin. Use ONLY 3% hydrogen peroxide. The foam gets warm: do not eat it, and wash your hands after.
Your bookRecord by table, labelled drawing or photo with captions. Explain the foam to a partner before you write.

STEP 2 · EXPLORE

What is a mixture?

8 – 18 min · Task 2 · Criterion A
  • A mixture is two or more substances mixed together but NOT chemically joined.
  • Each substance keeps its own properties: in a mix of iron and sulfur, the iron is still magnetic.
  • The amounts in a mixture can change (a little or a lot of sugar in tea).
  • Mixtures can be separated by physical methods such as sieving, filtering or using a magnet.
MixtureCompound
Substances are NOT chemically joinedElements ARE chemically joined
Each part keeps its own propertiesHas new properties
Amounts can changeFixed amounts (fixed formula)
Separated by physical methodsSeparated only by chemical reactions

2.2. How could you show that iron and sulfur powder is a mixture and not a compound? [1]

This step: 3 marks
Notes

Hydrogen peroxide slowly breaks down into water and oxygen gas. Yeast is a catalyst: it makes this happen very fast. The washing-up liquid traps the oxygen gas in bubbles, making foam.

STEP 3 · TEST

Practical: elephant toothpaste and mixture stations

18 – 38 min · Task 3 · Criterion C
  • 1. Mix 1 tablespoon of dry yeast with 3 tablespoons of warm water. Stir for 30 seconds.
  • 2. Using the funnel, pour 120 mL of 3% hydrogen peroxide into a 500 mL bottle standing on a tray.
  • 3. Add a squirt of washing-up liquid and a few drops of food colouring. Swirl gently.
  • 4. Pour the yeast mixture into the bottle and step back.
  • 5. Observe for 1 minute. Then touch the bottle (not the foam): is it warm?
  • 6. Part B: visit each station: salt water, sand + water, oil + water, sugar water, rice + beans, air (balloon).

STEP 4 · EXPLAIN

Homogeneous and heterogeneous

38 – 50 min · Task 4 · Criterion A
  • HOMOGENEOUS: the same all the way through. You cannot see the separate parts, even close up. Examples: salt water, sugar water, air, vinegar, tea.
  • HETEROGENEOUS: NOT the same all the way through. You can see the different parts. Examples: sand and water, salad, granite, oil and water, foam.
  • Tip: homo means SAME, hetero means DIFFERENT.
▶ Homogeneous vs heterogeneous mixtures (The Digital Classroom Experience, 4:18)What is the difference?

Notes

Milk looks the same all the way through. But under a microscope, you can see tiny drops of fat floating in water.
